# Documentation

The pages under `docs/` are this repository's source of truth for people and coding agents. This page says which page
owns each fact; read it before writing one.
<!-- cook:begin io.github.lmarqs.cookbook:docs#seed/kinds -->
<!-- io.github.lmarqs.cookbook:docs#seed --skills-root=.agents/skills --skills-root=.claude/skills -->
## Decisions, `adrs/`

Holds why the system is built as it is: each decision, the options weighed and why the choice won. Diátaxis type:
explanation.

- A record holds one foundation decision: other work is built on it, so reversing it changes more than one feature or
  module. It shapes structure, qualities, dependencies or interfaces, is hard to reverse, surprising to a reader new
  to its context and the result of a real trade-off.
- Not a record: how one feature is implemented, which its feature page or the code holds; a choice one change can
  reverse; a convention that static checking, such as linting, enforces, since its configuration already states it.
- The file is `NNNN-<slug>.md`, numbered in sequence; a deleted record's number is best left unused, since an old
  reference may still name it. The title names the decision taken.
- The lead says whom the decision concerns, the decision, and in a clause what moved it.
- Sections, in order: `Context`, what happened: the situation that raised the decision, what it cost and what was
  tried, then the forces the options are judged by; `Options`, each alternative and why it lost; `Decision`, the
  choice and why it won, with the product that implements it, if any, and why that one; `Consequences`, what becomes
  easier and what it costs.
- A record fits on about one page.
- A decision that changes is edited in place: it keeps its number, its title and slug follow the new choice, and
  `Options` keeps the previous choice and why it changed. A record is deleted when its decision is reversed outright,
  or when it fails the bar above, its facts moved to the page that owns them; version history keeps it.

## Interfaces, `api/`

Holds what an interface's contract file leaves out: who calls it and why, authentication, versioning, deprecation
policy and limits. Diátaxis type: reference.

- One page per interface. The lead says what the interface is for and who calls it.
- A `Contract` section names the definition file, an OpenAPI document, a proto file or a schema, and how the reference
  is built from it. The definition is the contract; the page links it.
- Design reasons live in `adrs/`, and the page links them.

## Architecture, `architecture.md`

Holds how the parts of the system fit together: the shape across its directories that no single file shows. Diátaxis
type: explanation.

- One page. The lead says what the system is and where its boundary is.
- Sections: `Parts`, each part with its responsibility and where it lives in the repository; `How they connect`, the
  dependencies and main flows, with diagrams where they help.
- Each structural choice links its record in `adrs/`; the page states no reasons for them. Interface rules, behavior and
  requirements live in their own kinds.

## Features, `features/`

Holds what the system does, one page per unit of behavior. Diátaxis type: reference.

- The lead says what the unit is and why it exists, or why it is as it is: what went wrong, or could not be done,
  without it.
- Sections follow the unit's own structure, and examples are welcome.
- The page describes. The options weighed for a foundation decision live in `adrs/` and the steps to operate the unit
  in `runbooks/`; the page links the records and runbooks that shaped it.
- A `Known limits` section, when the unit has any, lists what it doesn't handle, handles only partly or handles in a
  way that catches a reader out, each with its workaround. A limit is removed in the change that lifts it.

## Philosophy, `philosophy.md`

Holds the tenets that guide the decisions: what the team favors when options conflict. Diátaxis type: explanation.

- One page.
- A `Tenets` section: each tenet in one sentence, what it rules out, and links to the records in `adrs/` that apply it.
  A tenet that rules nothing out cannot guide a decision.
- A tenet guides many decisions; one decision applying it is a record in `adrs/`.

## Runbooks, `runbooks/`

Holds what to do when a trigger fires: an alert, a request or a symptom. Diátaxis type: how-to.

- One runbook per trigger, named after it.
- The lead states the outcome, one line on the impact, and the owner.
- Sections, in order: `Before you begin`, the tools and permissions; `Steps`, one action each with the output that
  shows it worked; `If it fails`, what to try and whom to call.
- A runbook links the pages that explain; its steps act. Steps that are a fixed list of commands become a script, and
  the runbook names it.
- A runbook is updated each time its trigger fires.

## UX, `ux/`

Holds the rules every interface follows, such as naming, messages and output. Diátaxis type: reference, normative.

- The lead states the scope: which interfaces the standard covers.
- Rules use MUST, SHOULD and MAY in capitals, and sparingly.
- Each rule carries its reason in one sentence, or links the record in `adrs/` that holds it.
- A standard is edited in place as its rules change.

The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT
RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in the standards under `ux/` are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14
(RFC 2119, RFC 8174) when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

## Where a fact goes

Each fact has one owning page: the page of the kind whose criteria above the fact meets. That page states the fact,
and every other page links to it. The link text names the fact, as in
`wait out [the rate limit](api/orders.md#limits)`, so the sentence reads without following the link. A summary
inside a page may repeat what the same page's body says.

## What a page holds

- What the repository shows nowhere else: the reason behind a choice, a convention, a rule and its scope. The code,
  contract files and version history hold their own facts, and a page links to them.
- What is true now, and why it is so.
- Its reasons, told as they happened: the situation as it was met, what it cost and what was tried, then the
  conclusion. "We need a queue" is a conclusion; "the payment call timed out inside the request, and customers who
  retried were charged twice" is a reason a reader can test. A decision record gives the options and the reasons, a
  rule gives its reason, and a reference page links the decisions that shaped it.
- Front matter holds keys a program reads, such as a site generator's.

## The lead

Every page opens, under its title, with its lead: what a reader needs to know about the page before reading it, in
this order:

1. Who reads it, and when they reach for it.
2. What it says.
3. Why it exists: what moved the team to write it, told as it happened.

A kind may name more for its lead. The lead is written last and read first: a page whose lead cannot be written is
not ready, and a body that says more or less than its lead fails review.

## Terms

Terms live in `glossary.md`: each entry is `**Term**:` with a definition of one or two sentences saying what the thing
is, then `_Avoid_:` with the synonyms the team rejected. It holds the terms specific to this project, one preferred
term per concept.

## Guides

A kind's directory appears with its first page, together with its guide, `README.md`: the kind's name as its title,
such as `# Decisions`, then a list linking each page with one sentence on it. A kind of one page appears with its
content.

## A new kind

A team declares a kind of its own on this page, outside the section the recipe writes, with a heading in the shape of
the ones above, ``## <Name>, `<directory>/` `` or ``## <Name>, `<page>.md` ``, then what it holds and what each page
must contain. A candidate passes every test first:

1. No kind above fits: for each, its facts fail a criterion that can be named.
2. Its facts have no other owner. An FAQ fails: each answer belongs to the feature or decision it explains.
3. It states what is true now, changing with its subject. A plan, a roadmap or a postmortem fails.
4. The repository shows it nowhere else: not the code, a contract file, version history or another tool's own file.
5. What each page must contain can be named, so a review can judge a page.

Facts that fail test 1 or 2 go to the kind above that owns them; facts that fail test 3 or 4 stay outside `docs/`.

## Skill

The `docs-layout` skill writes pages of each kind, adds terms and reviews the tree.
